sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Immediate Assessment of Abdominal Masses in Mid-Pregnancy
sections.description: This section introduces the patient’s presenting symptoms and teaches the initial bedside approach to a pregnant patient with abdominal pain, pelvic fullness, and dyspnoea. It emphasizes stabilization, obstetric considerations, and the value of careful physical and bimanual examination before advanced diagnostic reasoning begins.
subtopics: Key case features: nulliparity, maternal age in the 40s, obesity, and presentation at 21 weeks’ gestation
Symptom analysis: upper abdominal pain, pelvic pain, abdominal distension, and mild restrictive dyspnoea
Initial maternal assessment in pregnancy: vital signs, cardiopulmonary evaluation, and exclusion of immediate instability
Obstetric priorities during acute non-obstetric presentations: confirming fetal well-being and preserving pregnancy
Physical examination findings that raise concern for large intra-abdominal or pelvic masses
The diagnostic importance of bimanual vaginal examination in localizing pelvic masses during pregnancy
Supportive early management: analgesia, positioning, and symptom relief without unnecessary intervention
Interpreting associated inpatient findings: low-grade fever, urinary infection, inflammatory markers, and iron-deficiency anaemia
How pregnancy alters the clinical examination and may mask or distort abdominal mass findings

sections.section_title: Focused Diagnostic Workup for Complex Pelvic and Abdominal Masses During Pregnancy
sections.description: This section explains the safe and high-yield diagnostic tools available in pregnancy and how they were used in this case. It covers ultrasound, Doppler, non-contrast MRI, selected laboratory studies, and the limitations imposed by gestation on imaging interpretation and tumour marker use.
subtopics: Principles of evaluating adnexal and uterine masses during pregnancy
Ultrasound as first-line imaging: lesion size, location, wall characteristics, vascularity, and relationship to the uterus
Case ultrasound findings: two large unilocular cystic masses and a posterior uterine lesion with cystic degeneration
When and why to add colour Doppler in pregnancy-associated pelvic masses
Role of non-contrast MRI after ultrasound when anatomy is unclear or malignancy cannot be excluded
MRI safety in pregnancy: why gadolinium is generally avoided and why non-contrast imaging is preferred
Case MRI findings: thick walls, inhomogeneous fluid content, focal solid-appearing components, and unclear cleavage planes
Laboratory assessment relevant to this case: haemoglobin, ferritin, inflammatory markers, infection workup, and urine culture
Serum tumour markers in pregnancy: physiologic variability of CA-125 and limited diagnostic specificity
How uterine enlargement and mass effect reduce the accuracy of preoperative localization

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis and Clinical Reasoning: Distinguishing Leiomyoma From Adnexal Pathology
sections.description: This section walks the learner through the core diagnostic problem of the case: whether the masses were ovarian, endometriotic, or uterine in origin. It integrates imaging, anatomy, laboratory trends, and symptom mechanisms to show how clinicians balanced uncertainty, malignancy risk, and pregnancy-specific confounders.
subtopics: Constructing the differential diagnosis for large cystic masses in pregnancy
Decidualised endometrioma in pregnancy: pathophysiology, imaging features, and why it can mimic malignancy
Cystic or degenerating uterine leiomyoma: mechanisms of degeneration, atypical appearances, and pregnancy-related growth
Pedunculated subserosal leiomyoma as a common masquerader of adnexal masses
Features favoring ovarian or adnexal origin versus uterine origin on imaging and examination
The significance and limitations of a mildly rising CA-125 in the second trimester
Why dyspnoea was attributed to mechanical compression rather than primary cardiopulmonary disease
How torsion, leakage, ischaemia, or necrosis can explain pain and fever in a presumed mass lesion
Reasoning under uncertainty: why a definitive preoperative diagnosis remained difficult
How the team weighed benign possibilities against complications and the need to exclude oncologic disease

sections.section_title: Management Strategy in Pregnancy: When to Observe and When to Operate
sections.description: This section explains how management decisions were made once the masses were judged symptomatic and potentially complicated. It covers the general preference for conservative care in pregnancy, the indications that justified surgery in this case, operative planning, intraoperative decision-making, and the balance between diagnostic completeness and obstetric safety.
subtopics: General management principles for fibroids and adnexal masses during pregnancy
Indications for surgical intervention in pregnancy: severe symptoms, torsion, rupture, infection, concern for malignancy, or progressive mass effect
Why conservative treatment was insufficient in this patient
Choosing timing of surgery in the second trimester and its obstetric rationale
Selecting laparotomy versus laparoscopy: influence of gestational age, mass size, number, vascularity, and suspected intramural involvement
Preoperative counselling and informed consent in pregnant surgical patients
Intraoperative priorities: maternal safety, minimization of uterine manipulation, and fetal heart activity checks
Operative findings that changed the diagnosis: twisted, leaking, pedunculated cystic leiomyoma
Technique and rationale for limited myomectomy of the cranial mass while leaving the fixed caudal mass in situ
Use of peritoneal fluid sampling, antibiotic coverage, and progesterone support in the perioperative plan
Managing postoperative anaemia and transfusion decisions after myomectomy in pregnancy
How avoiding overtreatment can be as important as achieving tissue diagnosis

sections.section_title: Outcome, Delivery Planning, and Clinical Lessons for Future Practice
sections.description: This final section follows the patient from postoperative recovery through antenatal surveillance, pathology results, delivery planning, postpartum evolution, and broader clinical implications. It highlights how residual myoma anatomy influenced mode of delivery and distills the case into practical lessons for managing atypical masses in pregnancy.
subtopics: Postoperative maternal recovery and discharge after second-trimester laparotomy
Pathology confirmation of benign uterine leiomyoma with ischaemic necrosis near the twisted pedicle
Serial obstetric follow-up: fetal growth, amniotic fluid assessment, and surveillance of the residual pelvic mass
Natural history of leiomyomas during pregnancy and postpartum regression relevant to this case
How the residual caudal myoma affected labour mechanics and contraindicated vaginal birth
Rationale for elective caesarean delivery at 37 weeks using the prior surgical scar
Maternal and neonatal outcomes and postpartum symptom course
Shared decision-making regarding deferred postpartum surgery for residual leiomyoma
Clinical pearls: always consider pedunculated fibroid in the differential of an apparent adnexal mass in pregnancy
Imaging pearls: combine bimanual examination, ultrasound, and non-contrast MRI for complex masses
Management pearls: operate selectively for complications or oncologic concern, and tailor delivery mode to myoma size, number, and location
